text: Chapter 1. .

speaker: RAJESH
text: Dr. Nova, I’ve been thinking about what we learned in Lesson 1. We said imitation learning is the practical path forward - collect demonstrations, train a neural network, deploy on the robot. But I tried implementing a simple policy that predicts actions from observations, and something weird happened.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Ah, you’ve discovered the multimodal problem! Tell me what happened.

speaker: RAJESH
text: I collected 50 demonstrations of reaching around an obstacle. Sometimes I went left, sometimes I went right - both worked fine. But when I trained the network and deployed it... the robot went straight INTO the obstacle!

speaker: STUDENT_1
text: What is the focus of Lecture 2?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Deep Generative Modeling - specifically Variational Autoencoders (VAEs). Understanding VAEs is essential because ACT (Action Chunking Transformer) uses a VAE at its core.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: The VAE in ACT encodes demonstrations into a latent space, allowing sampling of coherent action chunks for your SO-ARM101 manipulation tasks.

speaker: STUDENT_2
text: So this lecture is all about VAEs - the mathematical foundation that lets robots handle multiple valid actions instead of averaging them?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Exactly.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: This is why Google's RT-2 and Figure 01's robots use VAE-based architectures at their core.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: laughs That’s the classic point estimate policy failure. Let me show you exactly why this happens.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: When your network outputs a single action - what we call a point estimate - it’s essentially computing the average of all the actions it saw in training. For that obstacle scenario, half your demos went left, half went right. The average? Straight ahead. Directly into the obstacle.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: A point estimate policy outputs a single “best” action. But when expert behavior is multimodal (multiple valid solutions), averaging produces an action that may not match ANY of the valid modes - often the worst possible choice.

speaker: STUDENT_2
text: What were the key takeaways from Lecture 1?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Classical robotics (FK/IK) fails on complex tasks. RL has safety/reward issues. Imitation learning is practical but point estimates cause mode averaging. We need distributions over actions.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: For SO-ARM101 folding: can't model fabric physics (classical fails), can't safely explore (RL fails), need multimodal policies from demos (IL + DGM).

speaker: STUDENT_3
text: So classical robotics fails on complex tasks, RL is too dangerous, and imitation learning works but has this mode averaging problem?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Precisely.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Tesla's Optimus team discovered this exact limitation when their early prototypes struggled with multimodal manipulation tasks.

speaker: RAJESH
text: So the problem isn’t the neural network or the training process - it’s the fundamental assumption that there’s one “correct” action?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Exactly! Let me give you another example. Imagine your SO-ARM101 bimanual setup folding a shirt. Sometimes you demonstrate folding the left side first, sometimes the right side first. Both are valid. But a point estimate policy might try to fold BOTH sides simultaneously - tangling the fabric because it’s averaging over incompatible strategies.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: The solution? Stop predicting THE action. Start predicting the DISTRIBUTION of possible actions.

speaker: STUDENT_3
text: Professor, quick review: fk vs ik?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: FK: joint angles to end-effector pose (easy, unique solution). IK: desired pose to joint angles (hard, multiple solutions). Both assume perfect model which doesn't exist.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: For example, with your SO-ARM101: SO-ARM101 IK might find 3 different joint configurations to reach the same fabric corner. Learning-based policies sidestep this by directly predicting actions.

speaker: STUDENT_4
text: FK is joints to position - straightforward. IK is position to joints - harder because there can be multiple solutions?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: That's right.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Boston Dynamics uses sophisticated IK solvers for Spot's leg movements, handling thousands of possible joint configurations.

speaker: RAJESH
text: That’s a huge shift in thinking! Instead of asking “what action should I take?”, we’re asking “what are ALL the actions I could take, and how likely is each one?”

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: You’ve got it. And this shift from point estimates to distributions is exactly what deep generative modeling gives us. It’s the key technology that makes modern robot policies like ACT (Action Chunking with Transformers) actually work.

speaker: STUDENT_4
text: Professor, quick review: why is rl problematic for real robot training?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Safety (random exploration breaks things), reward engineering (hard to define), sparse rewards (slow learning), generalization (overfits to exact conditions), sample inefficiency (needs millions of tries).

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: RL on SO-ARM101 would require thousands of fabric samples destroyed during exploration. Imitation learning needs maybe 100 demos.

speaker: STUDENT_1
text: So RL needs exploration, but exploration on real hardware means broken robots and safety issues?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Exactly.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: This is why Waymo does 99% of their RL training in simulation before ever touching a real car.

speaker: STUDENT_1
text: Professor, quick review: how does imitation learning work?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Expert demonstrates task to record (observation, action) pairs to train neural network to predict actions from observations to deploy policy on robot.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: You teleoperate Leader arms for 100 demos to train ACT on GPU to deploy to Follower arms. The policy has learned your folding technique.

speaker: STUDENT_2
text: Expert shows how, we record state-action pairs, train a neural network to copy the behavior?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Correct.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Sanctuary AI uses this exact approach - their teleoperators demonstrate tasks that robots learn to replicate.

speaker: STUDENT_2
text: Why do point estimate policies fail for imitation learning?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: They output single values, averaging over multimodal expert behavior. If experts sometimes go left, sometimes right, point estimate goes straight - often invalid.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Demos show both left-first and right-first folds. Point estimate outputs simultaneous both-arms motion that tangles the fabric.

speaker: STUDENT_3
text: If experts go left sometimes and right sometimes, the average is straight ahead - which could be the worst possible action!

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Exactly right.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: 1X Technologies learned this when their point estimate policies kept generating middle-ground actions that matched no valid behavior.

speaker: PROFESSOR
